# CUTLASS Build Script for PowerShell
# Created for RTX 4090 with CUDA 13.1

Write-Host "========================================"  -ForegroundColor Cyan
Write-Host "CUTLASS Build Script" -ForegroundColor Cyan
Write-Host "========================================" -ForegroundColor Cyan
Write-Host ""

# Set paths
$VS_PATH = "C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\2022\BuildTools\VC\Auxiliary\Build\vcvars64.bat"
$CMAKE_PATH = "C:\Program Files\CMake\bin\cmake.exe"
$NVCC_PATH = "C:\Program Files\NVIDIA GPU Computing Toolkit\CUDA\v13.1\bin\nvcc.exe"
$CUTLASS_ROOT = "C:\Users\User\OneDrive\Desktop\cutlass"

# Change to CUTLASS directory
Set-Location $CUTLASS_ROOT

# Step 1: Verify CUDA
Write-Host "[1/4] Verifying CUDA installation..." -ForegroundColor Yellow
if (Test-Path $NVCC_PATH) {
    & $NVCC_PATH --version
    Write-Host "CUDA OK" -ForegroundColor Green
} else {
    Write-Host "ERROR: CUDA compiler not found at $NVCC_PATH" -ForegroundColor Red
    exit 1
}
Write-Host ""

# Step 2: Create build directory
Write-Host "[2/4] Creating build directory..." -ForegroundColor Yellow
if (!(Test-Path "build")) {
    New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "build" | Out-Null
}
Set-Location "build"
Write-Host "Build directory ready" -ForegroundColor Green
Write-Host ""

# Step 3: Configure with CMake
Write-Host "[3/4] Configuring CUTLASS with CMake..." -ForegroundColor Yellow
Write-Host "This may take a few minutes..." -ForegroundColor Gray

$env:Path = "C:\Program Files\CMake\bin;C:\Program Files\NVIDIA GPU Computing Toolkit\CUDA\v13.1\bin;$env:Path"
$env:CUDA_PATH = "C:\Program Files\NVIDIA GPU Computing Toolkit\CUDA\v13.1"
$env:CUDA_PATH_V13_1 = "C:\Program Files\NVIDIA GPU Computing Toolkit\CUDA\v13.1"
$env:CudaToolkitDir = "C:\Program Files\NVIDIA GPU Computing Toolkit\CUDA\v13.1\"

# Import Visual Studio environment using a temporary batch file
$tempBatch = [System.IO.Path]::GetTempFileName() + ".bat"
$tempOut = [System.IO.Path]::GetTempFileName()

@"
@echo off
call "$VS_PATH"
set
"@ | Out-File -FilePath $tempBatch -Encoding ASCII

cmd /c "$tempBatch > `"$tempOut`""

# Parse environment variables
Get-Content $tempOut | ForEach-Object {
    if ($_ -match '^([^=]+)=(.*)$') {
        [System.Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable($matches[1], $matches[2], 'Process')
    }
}

Remove-Item $tempBatch, $tempOut

# Run CMake
& $CMAKE_PATH .. -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A x64 `
  -DCUTLASS_NVCC_ARCHS="89" `
  -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_EXAMPLES=ON `
  -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_TESTS=OFF `
  -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_PYTHON=OFF `
  -DCMAKE_CUDA_COMPILER="C:/Program Files/NVIDIA GPU Computing Toolkit/CUDA/v13.1/bin/nvcc.exe"

if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) {
    Write-Host "ERROR: CMake configuration failed" -ForegroundColor Red
    exit 1
}
Write-Host "Configuration complete" -ForegroundColor Green
Write-Host ""

# Step 4: Build
Write-Host "[4/4] Building CUTLASS..." -ForegroundColor Yellow

@echo off
REM CUTLASS Build Script for Windows
REM Created for RTX 4090 with CUDA 13.1

echo ========================================
echo CUTLASS Build Script
echo ========================================
echo.

REM Step 1: Set up Visual Studio environment
echo [1/5] Setting up Visual Studio environment...
call "C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\2022\BuildTools\VC\Auxiliary\Build\vcvars64.bat"
if %errorlevel% neq 0 (
    echo ERROR: Failed to load Visual Studio environment
    echo Make sure Visual Studio Build Tools 2022 is installed
    pause
    exit /b 1
)
echo.

REM Step 2: Verify CUDA
echo [2/5] Verifying CUDA installation...
"C:\Program Files\NVIDIA GPU Computing Toolkit\CUDA\v13.1\bin\nvcc.exe" --version
if %errorlevel% neq 0 (
    echo ERROR: CUDA compiler not found
    pause
    exit /b 1
)
echo.

REM Step 3: Create build directory
echo [3/5] Creating build directory...
if not exist build mkdir build
cd build
echo.

REM Step 4: Configure with CMake
echo [4/5] Configuring CUTLASS with CMake...
echo This may take a few minutes...
cmake .. -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A x64 ^
  -DCUTLASS_NVCC_ARCHS="89" ^
  -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_EXAMPLES=ON ^
  -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_TESTS=OFF ^
  -DCMAKE_CUDA_COMPILER="C:/Program Files/NVIDIA GPU Computing Toolkit/CUDA/v13.1/bin/nvcc.exe"

if %errorlevel% neq 0 (
    echo ERROR: CMake configuration failed
    pause
    exit /b 1
)
echo.

REM Step 5: Build
echo [5/5] Building CUTLASS...
echo This will take 10-30 minutes depending on your CPU...
echo.
cmake --build . --config Release -j 8

if %errorlevel% neq 0 (
    echo ERROR: Build failed
    pause
    exit /b 1
)

echo.
echo ========================================
echo Build Complete!
echo ========================================
echo.
echo Example executables are in:
echo %cd%\examples\
echo.
echo To test, run:
echo   .\examples\00_basic_gemm\Release\00_basic_gemm.exe
echo.
pause

The user is asking about the comment I made earlier regarding "explicit CUTLASS kernel selection" - I mentioned that FP16/BF16 efficiency was around 52% which is "typical for `torch.mm()` without explicit CUTLASS kernel selection." They want to know if this is worth exploring.

Let me think about what this means:

Currently, the benchmarks use `torch.mm()` which goes through PyTorch's dispatch mechanism - cuBLAS by default. CUTLASS kernels could potentially give better performance, especially for half-precision operations. But there are considerations:

1. The current approach (PyTorch torch.mm) is reliable and cross-platform
2. The CUTLASS Python API has known Windows issues (the `/usr/bin/which` problem mentioned in the plan)


3. We're only hitting about 172 TFLOPS on the RTX 4090 at FP16, which is well below the theoretical peak of 330.3 TFLOPS - so there's definitely room for improvement with properly tuned CUTLASS kernels optimized for SM89 architecture

This could be worth pursuing by either using CUTLASS Python bindings directly to launch GEMM kernels with specific tile and warp configurations, or leveraging PyTorch's built-in CUTLASS backend selection if available.

The real question is whether the complexity and potential Windows compatibility issues make this practical to implement, so I should give a balanced perspective on the tradeoffs.

content.text:
Worth considering. Here's the situation:

**Current state:** `torch.mm()` dispatches through cuBLAS. FP16/BF16 at ~52% efficiency means roughly half the tensor core throughput is being left on the table. FP32 exceeding theoretical peak suggests PyTorch is already sneaking in tensor core paths.

**What explicit CUTLASS kernel selection would give us:**
- Hand-tuned tile sizes and warp configs for SM89 (Ada Lovelace)
- Potentially 70-85% efficiency at FP16/BF16 instead of 52%
- Kernel autotuning for the specific matrix sizes your workflows actually use (ComfyUI attention layers, etc.)

**The catch:**
- CUTLASS Python API (`cutlass_cppgen`) has a known `/usr/bin/which` hardcoded call that breaks on Windows — this was explicitly deferred in the plan
- Direct CUTLASS kernel launches bypass PyTorch's memory allocator, which can cause fragmentation
- The payoff is mostly for sustained inference workloads (ComfyUI), not short bursts

**My read:** Not yet. The optimizer's job is to detect and recommend — the 52% efficiency number already triggers the right recommendations (TF32 override, CUDNN_BENCHMARK, CUTLASS_PATH for ComfyUI). Actual kernel selection is more of a ComfyUI-level integration (custom node or backend swap) than an optimizer concern.

If you want to chase those tensor core gains, the better path would be:
1. `torch.backends.cuda.preferred_linalg_library("cutlass")` — one-liner, if PyTorch 2.9 supports it
2. Or a ComfyUI custom node that swaps the GEMM backend per-model

Want me to check if PyTorch 2.9 exposes that CUTLASS backend flag?

Based on the web search results, here's what I found regarding PyTorch's CUTLASS backend and preferred linear algebra libraries:

## CUTLASS Backend in PyTorch

PyTorch 2.8 introduced Inductor CUTLASS backend support for both torch.compile and AOTInductor, as well as GEMMs such as mm, fp8 mm, addmm, and bmm. CUTLASS is an Nvidia header-only library that generates high-performance GEMMs with flexibility for fusions, including GEMM templates capable of instantiating thousands of kernels.

TorchInductor automates the autotuning process for all GEMMs in a model by precompiling kernels, caching them locally, and benchmarking them to select the optimal kernel for a given problem shape during model compilation, with generated kernels achieving state-of-the-art performance for some shapes.

## Current Challenges (2025)

However, recent discussions from March 2025 indicate ongoing challenges: CUTLASS is notorious for its lengthy compilation time, taking approximately 25 seconds to compile a single kernel, and can take around an hour to process all 10k+ configurations at the max instantiation level for each dtype and layout combination.

## Preferred Linear Algebra Library

Regarding `preferred_linalg_library`, users may use the environment variable TORCH_LINALG_PREFER_CUSOLVER=1 to set the preferred library to cuSOLVER globally. This is for linear algebra operations like eigenvalue decomposition, not GEMM operations handled by CUTLASS.

content.text:
Two different flags — and the CUTLASS path is a third:

**`preferred_linalg_library`** — cuSOLVER vs MAGMA. For linalg ops (SVD, eigenvalues, QR). **Not GEMMs.** Not what we want.

**`preferred_blas_library`** — cuBLAS vs cuBLASLt. Currently set to `cublas`. Switching to `cublaslt` could improve half-precision GEMM since cuBLASLt has better FP16/BF16 kernel selection. This is a one-liner we could test.

**CUTLASS via `torch.compile` Inductor** — PyTorch 2.8+ added CUTLASS as an Inductor backend. This is the real deal for kernel selection, but it requires `torch.compile()` wrapping and has a 25s-per-kernel compilation overhead. Best for ComfyUI models that run repeatedly, not for the optimizer itself.

**Quick win to test right now:** Let's see if switching to cuBLASLt improves half-precision throughput.

"C:/Python314/python.exe" -c "
import torch

device = torch.device('cuda:0')
torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = False

size = 4096
a = torch.randn(size, size, dtype=torch.float16, device=device)
b = torch.randn(size, size, dtype=torch.float16, device=device)

# Warmup
for _ in range(10):
    torch.mm(a, b)
torch.cuda.synchronize()

# cuBLAS (default)
torch.backends.cuda.preferred_blas_library('cublas')
start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
start.record()
for _ in range(20):
    torch.mm(a, b)
end.record()
torch.cuda.synchronize()
cublas_ms = start.elapsed_time(end) / 20
cublas_tflops = 2 * size**3 / (cublas_ms / 1000) / 1e12

# cuBLASLt
torch.backends.cuda.preferred_blas_library('cublaslt')
start2 = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
end2 = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
start2.record()
for _ in range(20):
    torch.mm(a, b)
end2.record()
torch.cuda.synchronize()
cublaslt_ms = start2.elapsed_time(end2) / 20
cublaslt_tflops = 2 * size**3 / (cublaslt_ms / 1000) / 1e12

print(f'FP16 4096x4096 GEMM:')
print(f'  cuBLAS:   {cublas_tflops:.1f} TFLOPS ({cublas_ms:.3f} ms)')
print(f'  cuBLASLt: {cublaslt_tflops:.1f} TFLOPS ({cublaslt_ms:.3f} ms)')
print(f'  Speedup:  {cublaslt_tflops/cublas_tflops:.2f}x')
"

content.text:
There it is: **"It is not supported on Windows."** cuBLASLt selection is experimental and doesn't actually switch on Windows — both paths hit the same cuBLAS kernels, hence the identical ~159 TFLOPS.

**Bottom line:**

| Path | Status | Windows Support |
|------|--------|-----------------|
| `preferred_blas_library("cublaslt")` | Experimental | Not supported |
| `preferred_linalg_library` | Works | Not for GEMMs |
| `torch.compile` + CUTLASS Inductor | PyTorch 2.8+ | Works, but 25s/kernel compile overhead |

The only viable path for explicit CUTLASS kernel selection on Windows is **`torch.compile` with the Inductor CUTLASS backend**. That's a ComfyUI-level change (wrapping model forward passes), not something the optimizer should own. The 52% FP16 efficiency we're seeing is the cuBLAS ceiling on this platform for raw `torch.mm()`.

**Recommendation:** Park this. The optimizer is doing its job — detecting the efficiency gap and recommending the right env vars. Actual kernel swaps belong downstream in the inference tools (ComfyUI, etc.).
